items.excerpt: #### ‘Dimagi Naxals’ instigating people against Constitution and democracy: PM Modi as Maoists eliminated Targeting political opponents, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said armed Maoists had been eliminated, but “dimagi Naxals” (ideological supporters) had infiltrated several political parties and organisations and were instigating people against the Constitution and democracy. “We must identify and defeat such elements and secure the country,” Mr. Modi said, while celebrating Deepavali with security personnel at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) camp in Bastar, Chhattisgarh. #### Congress donations fall nearly 75%, sharpest decline in a decade The Congress party's receipts from donations above ₹20,000 plunged nearly 75% to ₹130.69 crore in 2025-26, the steepest annual fall in such contributions in a decade, an analysis of the party's filings with the Election Commission shows. Of the 54 monitoring stations across the city, 24 recorded 'severe' air quality, while the remaining stations were in the 'very poor' category. items.title: AP News Summary at 12:57 p.m. EST | National | guardonline.com
items.excerpt: Collision between 2 trains in Egypt kills 7 and injures more than 100 CAIRO (AP) — Two trains collided south of Cairo, killing seven people and injuring over 100 others, according to the Egyptian Chief Prosecutor’s office. The crash happened Sunday in al-Ayyat district, in Giza province. A train traveling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a stationary train heading to Aswan. Investigators arrived at the site late Sunday. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, with a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi ordered a prompt investigation. Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to clear the wreckage and restore services. JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog has formally given opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government. While complex coalition negotiations still lie ahead, this is a significant step in the former military chief’s effort to oust Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. It comes after elections were held in a deeply divided country scarred by the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, and the multifront wars they triggered. The announcement doesn’t guarantee that Eisenkot will become the next prime minister. He has up to six weeks to form a government by securing alliances, a daunting challenge because the Oct. 27 election gave neither his bloc nor Netanyahu’s a clear majority in parliament. WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters have sent a strong election-year message to President Donald Trump and the new Democratic congressional majority to repair the U.S. economy damaged by inflation. Trump insists the economy is booming and claims he's willing to work with Democrats, though he hasn't done much of that in the past. After a strong jobs report last week, Trump remains defiant and promises to veto anything that he thinks would hurt the country. Democrats are preparing for early fights on government spending, budget deficits, tariffs and Social Security. Rising prices continue to make middle-class lives less affordable. That poses political risks for both parties in future elections. KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Poland is in mourning after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15. The attack happened Saturday in Main Square, a major tourist hub. Police shot and wounded the attacker, who is also linked to three other deaths at his family home. Authorities describe the incident as an “act of terror.” The square remained partially closed Sunday as investigations continued. Two police officers who stopped the gunman are hospitalized, one in critical condition.

items.title: US inflation set to cool in October after two months of sharp increases | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: 8 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 1:03 PM IST By Vince Golle and Craig Stirling Prices for US goods and services probably rose at a slower pace in October after two particularly uncomfortable months for American consumers. The consumer price index is seen rising 0.3% after a 0.6% increase that was the largest since April, based on the median projection in a Bloomberg survey of economists ahead of Tuesday’s Bureau of Labor Statistics’ release. The core measure, which excludes often-volatile energy and food components, also probably cooled. The survey median sees a 0.2% increase for October, which would be the smallest advance in three months. The agency won’t publish year-over-year figures after it skipped the October 2025 CPI release due to the federal government shutdown at the time. ## The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. Warsh will have to explain why ## Fed Chair Warsh stresses price stability, offers no signals on rate outlook The October CPI will be the last before the Federal Reserve’s meeting in December, at which investors expect policymakers to boost interest rates. Economists will also assess the finer details of the report for clues on inflation risks into early 2027. Economists at Citigroup Inc. said in a recent note that they anticipate limited pass-through of high energy costs to goods prices, as well as moderate services inflation. What Bloomberg Economics Says... > “We expect headline CPI slowed to 0.25% in October (vs. 0.65% prior). The core likely softened to 0.24% (vs. 0.33% prior), with both softer goods and services price gains driving the improvement. For goods, used cars and consumer electronics — categories that have faced pressure from the AI boom — saw slower inflation. For services, gains in owners’ equivalent rent are down a third from a September spike.” > > > > —Anna Wong, Troy Durie and Eliza Winger The latest snapshot of inflation also follows Friday’s stronger-than-expected October jobs report. Sustained employment growth has the potential of ensuring consumers keep spending, while allowing the Fed to keep its focus squarely on inflation. Another price report, due on Friday, is projected to show nagging inflationary pressures faced by companies. The producer price index is forecast to accelerate to 6.6% for the year through October, the steepest annual increase in nearly four years.

items.excerpt: Published : Nov. 8, 2026 - 10:24:06 ... A stronger-than-expected US jobs report bolstered the case for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, which had lost some momentum ‌amid a post-election stock market selloff and growing fears that weaker AI-driven demand could undercut the economy. Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, more than twice what economists had expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Friday, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent. Average hourly wages gained 3.1 percent from a year earlier, not enough to keep up with a 3.7 percent rise in consumer prices that is ‌taking a bigger chunk of the typical paycheck's purchasing power. After the US central bank left its policy rate on hold last month, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said policymakers would be watching for "the accumulation of data" to help decide whether more monetary policy tightening would be needed. For San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, the latest monthly jobs report appeared to put a definitive tick in the "yes" column. "People are just at the point where they're — they say 'Inflation — I'm doing well ⁠in everything, except I can't keep up with inflation,' so that has to be our number one priority, and the fact that we have a solid labor market gives us the latitude, really, to just get that job done," Daly said in an interview on CNBC. "My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," said Daly, who is not a voting member of the Fed's policy committee this ⁠year but typically voices views similar to the majority view. Noting "how volatile the world seems to be in many ways," she added, "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head. But more is likely to be ​needed and certainly we're prepared — I'm prepared — to do that, if that's what the economy calls for." In comments at a St. Louis civic event Friday, St. ‌Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remained the top concern in his conversations with businesses in his district. "Inflation is a regressive tax, a distortionary tax," said Musalem, who has advocated for further rate ‌increases. "The best thing we can do for growth ‌and employment is bring inflation back down on a timely basis." He did not address a recent swoon in stock markets driven lower by new doubts about ‌the pace and sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom, but said for now he feels the emerging ​industry is feeding higher inflation through demand for commodities such as copper. ... items.title: US inflation, housing and jobs: 4 key economic updates to watch this week - The Times of India
items.excerpt: Edited by Shivanghi Payal / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 08, 2026, 14:27 IST ... The focus comes as American households continue to deal with high prices of everyday essentials, from petrol to groceries. The latest updates follow the US midterm elections, in which Democrats swept Congress, a week ago. The economic situation has also been shaped by the war between the US and Iran, which began in February and cut global oil supplies. The resulting rise in energy costs added to inflationary pressures that were already high because of President Donald Trump's unpredictable tariff conflict with much of the world. Economists, investors and policymakers will be watching the upcoming numbers to assess how the war and tariffs continue to affect prices, the housing market and employment. ## US inflation: October CPI and PPI figures in focus The first major update will come on Tuesday, when the US releases its consumer price index (CPI) data for October. Economists expect inflation to rise to 3.9%, against 3.7% in September. The CPI tracks price movements across a broad range of goods and services. Inflation has remained above 3% since March, following the start of the US war with Iran in February. The conflict led to a sharp rise in energy prices, which pushed up petrol prices and shipping costs. Businesses will also get a fresh reading of their costs on Friday, when the October producer price index (PPI) is released. Unlike the CPI, the PPI measures price changes before goods and services reach consumers. The September PPI report had recorded its biggest increase since December 2022. It also showed how higher fuel costs, particularly for diesel, were feeding into shipping and warehousing expenses. However, crude prices fell sharply over the past week after the US midterm elections. Some believe Democrats, who routed President Donald Trump's GOP, will push to end the Iran conflict, which has sent energy prices soaring.

items.title: PCE inflation accelerates to 3.6% as GDP growth beats estimates, jobless claims fall – Trade Talk Journal
items.excerpt: November 8, 2026 US inflation accelerated in September, while economic growth exceeded expectations in the third quarter and jobless claims remained near multi-decade lows, presenting the Federal Reserve with a challenging policy outlook. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the central bank’s preferred inflation gauge, increased 0.5% month-on-month on a seasonally adjusted basis, taking the annual rate to 3.6%, according to Commerce Department data released Thursday. The monthly increase matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below expectations. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from the previous month and 3.1% annually. Both readings were in line with economists’ forecasts. Fed officials generally view core inflation as a better indicator of longer-term price pressures, although they monitor both measures. Inflation remains significantly above the Fed’s 2% target, even as the economy continues to demonstrate resilience. ## Economic growth exceeds expectations The Commerce Department report showed that US gross domestic product increased at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% estimate and accelerating from 2.2% growth in the second quarter. Consumer spending, a key driver of the US economy, increased 0.5% in September, slightly below the 0.6% gain forecast by economists. Personal income rose 0.2%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% increase. The combination of firm economic growth and persistent inflation could make it harder for policymakers to justify easing monetary policy in the near term. The data arrived a day after the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75%-4.00%. Officials have said they can assess incoming economic information before deciding on their next move, despite inflation remaining elevated. “The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that’s happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said. Thursday’s figures, however, suggest that policymakers may have more work to do to bring inflation under control while sustaining economic growth.

items.title: Live updates: Trump offers press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White
items.excerpt: ## What to know today - WILES OUT: President Donald Trump announced Friday that his chief of staff Susie Wiles would leave her role this week and would be replaced by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. - DEMOCRATIC PRIORITIES: Democrats are weighing what they should do with control of the next Congress. While some have called for investigations of Trump administration officials others have called on Democrats to focus on affordability policies. - VOTE COUNTING: Votes are still being tallied in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races. Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom continue to narrowly lead their Republican opponents, GOP Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith, respectively. ## Hakeem Jeffries says he is a 'hard yes' on impeaching Hegseth House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said in an interview on ABC's "This Week" that he supports a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Nathan Posner / Anadolu via Getty Asked whether he would support an impeachment resolution of Hegseth by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., Jeffries said he was a "hard yes." "The so-called Secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said. "Pete Hegseth has got to go." Asked whether he believed all other House Democrats would support the resolution, Jeffries said, "We'll certainly have that conversation on Tuesday morning." He added though that he believed there would be "incredibly strong support" for the effort. Massie, a strong critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran, has been trying to push for the secretary's impeachment. He initially filed an impeachment resolution in September, but Republican leaders canceled votes and lawmakers left early, pushing the vote to after midterms. ## Sen. Bernie Sanders 'not worried' about Stephen Miller as White House chief-of-staff During an interview on NBC News' "Meet the Press," Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said he was open to working with Trump to solve cost-of-living issues for Americans, adding that he's "not worried," that the president's new chief of staff could block meaningful work from getting done. ... "I think when Trump looks out in the world, and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage," Sanders said. "He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does: guaranteeing health care to all people." "So I’m not worried about Miller," the senator added." Do I think we can work with Trump? Maybe. I’m not by no means guaranteeing it, but it is certainly worth the effort." Following Democrats' sweeping victories in Tuesday's midterm elections, Trump said he'd be open to working with Democrats in Congress to make deals. On Friday, asked directly where he sees opportunities to work with Democrats, the president told reporters, "I think a lot." He added, "I mean, I said before, immigration’s one, tax cuts, or maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient and better. A lot of economic development initiatives we can do. I think we can do a lot of things together.”

items.excerpt: ### Doctor Who: the Paternoster Gang head to the Silurian age in The Misplaced World - What happened: Big Finish has announced The Paternoster Gang: The Misplaced World, a two-hour, feature-length audio drama starring Neve McIntosh as Madame Vastra, Catrin Stewart as Jenny and Dan Starkey as Strax - The story: While chasing a ruthless animal smuggler, the trio are thrown back tens of millions of years to a pivotal point in Silurian history, when Vastra’s people rule the Earth but are preparing for what they believe is the end of their society. Vastra must decide how much to change her own race’s past, and Jenny meets her wife’s former lover - The Doctor’s part: Paul McGann appears as the Eighth Doctor, who sets the Gang off on their dangerous mission - Who’s making it: McIntosh and Starkey wrote it themselves. Script editor Matt Fitton describes it as a mash-up of Conan Doyle’s The Lost World and the stop-motion monster movies of the 1970s - UK availability: Released by Big Finish in December 2026; available to pre-order now as a download (£13.99) or download plus a limited 1,000-copy collector’s CD (£21.99) ... - What happened: Adam Driver told Jimmy Kimmel Live! that joining Marvel Studios’ X-Men as the villain Mister Sinister “felt like the right time”, after years of turning down roles in the MCU, Variety reported - Why now: Driver said he was a big fan of the X-Men and was won over by director Jake Schreier’s idea for the film, by Kevin Feige and by the script, which he called “really cool”. He admitted he had been wary of Marvel because if a film that big is bad, “a lot of people will see you ... - What happened: Prime Video has released the first teaser and first-look images for Criminal, an eight-episode series based on Ed Brubaker and Sean Phillips’ Eisner Award-winning comics, starring Charlie Hunnam, Adria Arjona, Emilia Clarke and Luke Evans, Prime Video and Deadline reported

items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 8, 2026 - 47 mins ago ... 'Godzilla Minus Zero' stomps to a record-setting $31.6 debut, clobbering 'The Cat in the Hat' NEW YORK (AP) — “Godzilla Minus Zero” stomped into movie theaters with a chart-topping $31.6 million over the weekend, scoring a record debut for a foreign-language film at the North American box office. Takashi Yamazaki‘s “Godzilla Minus One” sequel easily thrashed Warner Bros.' animated “The Cat in the Hat.” That film, featuring the voice of Bill Hader, opened with $20.5 million. Third place went to Angel Studios’ “Drummer Boy,” with $9.3 million on its opening weekend. The Oscar-contending “Wild Horse Nine” notched Martin McDonagh's best opening weekend, with $6 million. The weekend also saw the widest North American release for an Indian film. The Hindi epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” launched with $12.2 million domestically and $32 million in India. LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand's convictions this week for rape and sexual assault have renewed scrutiny on the BBC and other media employers that may have looked the other way. Brand, who gained fame while cultivating an outrageous persona, was convicted Thursday on multiple charges involving several women. The BBC has apologized for a culture that allowed his behavior to go unchecked. An internal probe followed a joint investigation by The Times and Channel 4, which aired accusations from women who said they were abused by Brand. Analysts argue that Brand's raunchy image acted as a shield, allowing his excesses to be overlooked by employers and the public, too. LONDON (AP) — Fictional spymaster George Smiley is back in "The Taper Man," a new thriller set in the world of John le Carré and written by his son, Nick Harkaway. The novel follows Smiley to the U.S. in 1965, chasing a Soviet agent. Harkaway says writing a Cold War story in 2026 feels like “writing in the mirror” due to modern parallels. The book, published Nov. 17 in the U.S., is Harkaway’s second le Carré novel since his father’s death in 2020. Harkaway, who grew up with his father's stories, captures the le Carré spirit, blending espionage with office politics. He plans to write at least one more Smiley book and says other writers may be invited to expand the universe. TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old father of Prince Harry’s wife Meghan, has been arrested by federal agents in Florida and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material in California. Thomas Markle was released after a court appearance in Tampa. Authorities say a search of storage units in the Los Angeles area turned up dozens of items. There was no immediate comment from his lawyer. Meghan Markle had recently said she's “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images were found at her father’s former home in the Philippines. NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm a Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition).” It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. NEW YORK (AP) — Siân Heder's follow-up to the best picture-winning “CODA” chronicles the disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann. Heumann died at the age of 75 in 2023 while Heder was developing the movie with her. She resolved to push on with the project to honor Heumann and try to bring some of her accessibility gains to the movie industry. Characters with disabilities remain extremely uncommon in Hollywood productions, and big-screen biopics like “Being Heumann” are even more seldom. “Being Heumann,” starring Ruth Madeley as Heumann, features the largest ensemble ever of performers with disabilities. SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52. His family announced his death Friday on Instagram, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause. Lelio was known for his groundbreaking film “A Fantastic Woman,” which portrayed a transgender woman and won the Academy Award for best international film. It was Chile's second Oscar win. Lelio’s other works include "Gloria," "The Wonder," and “Disobedience.” He had begun filming “Poeta Chileno” in September. Born in Argentina, Lelio moved to Chile at age two and studied at the Chilean Film School.

items.title: Movie News: 8th November 2026
items.excerpt: Pattinson and Hoult join the Bond screen tests: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult have been added to the list of actors who screen-tested for the next James Bond, according to Deadline, which says they joined Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner in the final screen tests. The Hollywood Reporter says Pattinson’s test took place in London on the weekend of 24 October, while he’s filming The Batman Part II, as I mentioned when it paused in October. Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman films. Both reports are unconfirmed, and there’s no timeline yet, although most expect a decision by the end of the year. The Sun has claimed that O’Connor has won the part, which NME has described as a rumour. It’s the first Bond film since Amazon bought the franchise’s creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. Ramayana’s Diwali weekend: Nitesh Tiwari’s epic Ramayana: Part 1 had a big start in India, but its first Friday saw a 26% drop. According to Sacnilk, it took ₹48.05 crore net on Friday (about $5 million), taking its India net total to ₹112.90 crore (about $12 million), and its worldwide gross to ₹221.05 crore (about $23 million) after two days. The makers claimed that its opening day gross worldwide was ₹155 crore, against Sacnilk’s estimate of ₹127.5 crore. Hindi accounts for about 73.5% of its India net. The film is the first of a two-part retelling of the epic, with Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash, and Diwali weekend should show whether it can bounce back. I’ll bring you the full opening-weekend numbers tomorrow. Nollywood’s ₦1 billion streak: In Nigeria, Agbara Nla: The Return was number one for a fifth consecutive weekend, with ₦27.4 million (about $21,000) from 4,781 admissions, taking its total to ₦450.1 million (about $338,000) from 75,444 admissions and closing in on the all-time Nollywood top ten. Cinemas as a whole took about ₦130.7 million (about $98,000) over the weekend, and October ended with ₦1.19 billion (about $895,000), the 11th consecutive month above ₦1 billion since December 2025. The Far East: Tokyo’s winners: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival closed on Wednesday, with the Tokyo Grand Prix going to Milcho Manchevski’s Sister Brother Manhole Cover, a co-production between North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Albania, Italy and the UK, which comes with a $19,000 prize. Sun Xun’s animated feature Magic Atlas, a Singapore production, won the Special Jury Prize, and Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso took Best Director for Double Freedom. The Kurosawa Akira Award went to Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof, whom I mentioned at the Cate Blanchett screening, and Japan’s Mipo O. The festival showed 204 films to 69,072 people.
